bib.title: Generating Sequences With Recurrent Neural Networks

question: Can stacked LSTM networks generate complex sequences with long-range structure, for discrete text and real-valued handwriting, by next-step prediction, and be conditioned on a text string whose alignment is unknown?
hypothesis: A better memory (LSTM) is a more effective route to stable, long-range-coherent sequence generation than injecting noise into predictions.
contributions: Deep stacked LSTM prediction network with skip connections, trained for next-step prediction on text (word and character level) and handwriting
Mixture density output layer for real-valued pen traces
A soft-window convolutional mechanism letting a recurrent network condition on a character string with unknown alignment (handwriting synthesis)
Probability-biased sampling and primed sampling for legibility and style mimicry

method.summary: Stacked LSTM RNN with input-to-hidden and hidden-to-output skip connections trained by BPTT to predict the next input. Softmax outputs for text, mixture-of-bivariate-Gaussians plus Bernoulli outputs for pen offsets. For synthesis a Gaussian-mixture soft window over the one-hot text is output by hidden layer 1 and fed back to all layers.
method.task: next-step sequence prediction and generation (text, online handwriting), conditional handwriting synthesis

datasets.name: Penn Treebank (WSJ)
datasets.preprocessing: vocabulary limited to 10,000 words, rest mapped to unknown token; end-of-sentence token included in input and loss; start-of-sentence ignored

datasets.name: Hutter Prize Wikipedia (enwik8)
datasets.split: first 96M bytes split into sequences of 100 bytes; remaining 4M validation
datasets.preprocessing: 205 one-byte symbols, predicted one byte at a time; sequences not shuffled

datasets.name: IAM-OnDB
datasets.size: 5364 / 1438 / 1518 / 3859 lines (train / val1 / val2 / test) from 775 / 192 / 216 / 544 forms
datasets.split: train + test + larger validation set used for training; smaller validation set for early stopping; no independent test set
datasets.preprocessing: each line one sequence; x,y offsets normalised to mean 0 std 1; inputs size 3 (dx, dy, end-of-stroke); synthesis uses 57 characters (80 reduced, digits and most punctuation mapped to non-letter)

models.name: Byte LSTM, Wikipedia
models.context: state reset every 100 sequences (up to 10K characters of history); gradient truncated to 100 bytes

models.name: Handwriting prediction net
models.architecture: stacked LSTM + 20-component bivariate Gaussian mixture density output
models.init_from: 3-layer retrained with adaptive weight noise (std init 0.075)

other.output_layer: 121 (20 weights, 40 means, 40 std devs, 20 correlations, 1 end-of-stroke)

other.window: 10 Gaussians, size 30 parameter vector, window vector size 57

training.objective: negative log likelihood of next input, L(x) = -sum log Pr(x_{t+1}|y_t); BPTT
training.optimizer: Penn and Wikipedia: SGD with momentum (0.99 Penn, 0.9 Wikipedia); handwriting: rmsprop variant (decay 0.95, momentum 0.9, lr 0.0001, epsilon 0.0001)
training.epochs: Penn char 9 (none) / 25 (weight noise) / 26 (adaptive); word 11 / 14; Wikipedia: four epochs to converge
training.regularisation: Penn: weight noise std 0.075 per training sequence, or adaptive weight noise (Graves 2011), each initialised from the previous less regularised network; handwriting: adaptive weight noise init std 0.075 (fixed-variance weight noise ineffective)

other.gradient_clipping: Penn/Wikipedia: LSTM derivatives clipped to [-1,1]; handwriting: output derivatives [-100,100], LSTM derivatives [-10,10]
other.dynamic_evaluation: weights adapt while the test data is predicted, seen once
other.rmsprop_eq: Eqs 38-41 with decay 0.95, momentum 0.9, lr 0.0001, epsilon 0.0001

inference.decoding: ancestral sampling from the output distribution, fed back as next input; optional probability-biased sampling
inference.max_tokens: samples 700 timesteps for prediction network (Fig 11); synthesis stops when phi(t,U+1) > phi(t,u) for all u<=U
inference.prompting: primed sampling: clamp inputs to a real sequence for first T steps with character string c'=c+s

parameters.probability_bias_b: sigma=exp(sigma_hat - b), pi proportional to exp(pi_hat (1+b)); b=0 is unbiased; 0.15 'slight bias'; 1 used with priming (Figs 20-21)

metrics.name: bits-per-character
metrics.definition: average -log2 Pr(x_{t+1}|y_t) over the test set

metrics.name: perplexity
metrics.definition: 2 to the power of the average bits per word; approx 25.6^BPC for Penn

metrics.name: Log-Loss
metrics.definition: mean of L(x) per sequence for handwriting

baselines: 5-gram Keyser-Ney, feedforward NN, PAQ8, dynamically evaluated word RNN and ensembles (Mikolov 2012 thesis numbers)
eval.protocol: validation set only for handwriting, no independent test set; single runs, no seeds or significance tests stated; informal human blind tests for handwriting realism

availability.data: IAM-OnDB, Penn Treebank, Hutter Prize data are existing public datasets

results.claim: Wikipedia byte-level 7x700 LSTM reaches 1.33 BPC on validation with dynamic evaluation, against 1.67 static.
results.setup: Hutter Prize first 100M bytes, 96M train / 4M val, 7 layers x 700 LSTM, SGD lr 0.0001 mom 0.9

results.claim: Hutter Prize winner (PAQ-8 variant) gets 1.28 BPC including decompressor code, so the LSTM does not beat it.
results.note: source is Knoll and de Freitas 2011

results.claim: On Penn Treebank the best char-level LSTM (weight noise, dynamic eval) reaches 1.24 BPC, perplexity 124.
results.setup: Penn Treebank test set, 1x1000 LSTM, weight noise 0.075, dynamic evaluation
results.table: Table 1, row char weight noise dynamic yes, column BPC 1.24, Perplexity 124

results.claim: Best word-level LSTM on Penn (weight noise, dynamic eval) reaches perplexity 117.
results.setup: Penn Treebank test, 1x1000 LSTM word level, 10,000 vocab
results.table: Table 1, row word weight noise dynamic yes, column Perplexity 117

results.claim: Dynamic evaluation helped LSTM far more than Mikolov reports for RNNs (124.7 to 123.2).
results.setup: Mikolov thesis word-level RNN with dynamic evaluation
results.quote: he records a perplexity improvement from 124.7 to 123.2 with word-level RNNs

results.claim: Three-layer handwriting prediction net with adaptive weight noise has validation log-loss -1057.7 nats.
results.setup: IAM-OnDB validation, 3x400 LSTM, 20 mixture components, rmsprop
results.table: Table 3, row 3 layer adaptive weight noise, column Log-Loss

results.claim: Synthesis network with adaptive weight noise reaches log-loss -1128.2 and SSE 0.23, SSE 44% lower than the best prediction network.
results.setup: IAM-OnDB validation, 3x400 LSTM, 10-Gaussian soft window, 57 characters
results.table: Table 4, row adaptive weight noise, column Log-Loss

results.claim: Synthesis soft window uses offsets kappa_t = kappa_{t-1} + exp(kappa_hat), which made alignment possible.
results.setup: Handwriting synthesis, soft window of 10 Gaussians

results.claim: Fixed-variance weight noise was ineffective for the handwriting mixture density net.
Priming and probability bias 0.15 give a balance between diversity and legibility.

limits: No independent test set for handwriting; validation results may be overfit (authors concede).
No benchmark results exist for IAM-OnDB, so no baselines for handwriting; realism judged by eye and informal blind tests by the author.
Penn word vs char comparison unfair: 54M vs 4.3M weights.
Wikipedia: LSTM at 1.33 BPC does not beat the Hutter Prize winner 1.28; gradient truncated to 100 bytes so approximate.
Samples do not make sense beyond short phrases (Wikipedia).
Batch size, seeds, hardware, compute and code not stated.
Forward-only monotone window (kappa offsets > 0) cannot reorder; unsuited to tasks needing reordering (inferred from Eq 51).

terms.definition: allow the network to adapt its weights as it is being evaluated (so long as it only sees the test data once)
discrete convolution of the character sequence with a mixture of K Gaussians whose parameters are output by the network
